claims.text: Near-simultaneous reduction of multiple noble-metal precursors promotes formation of single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
With limited free-atom mobility, increasing the number of atom types makes random-alloy formation more likely.
Rapid kinetic locking can preserve a random multimetal arrangement before phase segregation occurs.
The proposed starting material is a solid mixture containing at least five noble-metal precursors.
The precursor metals are present in stoichiometric proportions.
A controlled multistep thermal profile can synchronize the distinct precursor-reduction events while limiting atomic diffusion.
Moderate temperatures and short dwell times reduce overall atomic mobility.
Reduced mobility prevents prolonged diffusion and thereby suppresses phase separation.
Particle formation occurs through co-nucleation of diverse metal species in a constrained environment.
The constrained formation pathway produces a disordered solid solution rather than segregated domains.
Close temporal proximity of reduction causes the metals to intermix stochastically.
Restricted free-atom movement fixes the intermixed metals into a single phase rather than allowing equilibrium phase separation.
The resulting nanoparticles will have homogeneous elemental distributions and a single-phase high-entropy lattice.
The nanoparticles will maintain high surface area and compositionally uniform catalytic sites.
The nanoparticle composition will deviate minimally from the intended stoichiometry.
A longer, higher-temperature treatment of the same precursor composition will cause partial segregation or multiphase regions by increasing diffusion.
The mechanism applies primarily to metals having low enthalpy of mixing and relatively similar atomic radii.
The mechanism may fail for strongly immiscible components or extreme rapid-heating methods.
Short-range ordering, elemental volatility, or strong enthalpic interactions may disrupt random mixing and cause compositional inhomogeneity.

contradictions.description: The conditions field says reduced mobility minimizes the driving force for phase separation, whereas the mechanism treats reduced mobility as a kinetic barrier that prevents an equilibrium thermodynamic driving force from being realized. Mobility changes kinetics, not necessarily the thermodynamic driving force.
